case_title: Bhaikon @ Bakul Borah v. State of Assam
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony; corroborative witness testimony (father, brothers, co-villagers); medical (post-mortem) evidence; recovery of stained underwear and FSL examination
aggravating_circumstances: Heinous crime of rape and murder; body dumped in a place surrounded by bushes and shrubs
mitigating_circumstances: Young age (33) and High Court's finding that the case was not rarest of rare
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under ss.302 and 376 IPC; death sentence for s.302; life RI for s.376 with fine of Rs.10,000
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed and conviction confirmed; death sentence altered to life imprisonment (s.302) with fine of Rs.1,000; s.376 sentence altered to 7 years
neutral_facts: According to the prosecution, on the afternoon of 29 March 2000 the victim, a 22-year-old woman, went to a field near an embankment to attend her goats. When she did not return home, her father searched for her along the embankment. While returning, he heard loud laughter from a farm house belonging to the accused. Later he went back to the embankment, shouted for her, and the accused came out of the farm house and looked at him. The father then went down a path and found the victim lying dead on the left side, with a cut injury on her chin and blood oozing from her body. He raised an alarm, and her brother and other villagers gathered. The accused also came to the spot and enquired. The body was taken home, and a Sub-Inspector of Police seized the victim's clothing and prepared a seizure list. The inquest was held and the body was sent for post-mortem. The brother lodged a written complaint at the police out-post, and a case was registered. During investigation, the victim's underwear stained with semen was seized the same day. The accused and an eyewitness labourer were apprehended and interrogated. On the next day, police seized a blue underwear of the accused suspected to have semen stains, a bed sheet, a sporting item and a dao from the farm house. Both underwear items were sent for forensic examination. The post-mortem doctor found death by asphyxia due to throttling, a fractured trachea, bruises on the neck and a cut injury on the chin, and found no spermatozoa in the vaginal smear and no sign of injury on the genital organs. The eyewitness stated that he saw the accused and a companion follow the victim, saw them commit rape and then throttle her, and saw them drag the body into bushes. He said he stayed silent out of fear because both men carried khukris. The victim's father, two brothers and co-villagers gave corroborative evidence about the body and the scene.
physical_harm: Death by asphyxia due to throttling; cut injury over lower chin with cut to mandible; bruises on neck; fractured trachea
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness testimony of PW-1; corroborative testimony of PW-2 (father of deceased) and brothers; post-mortem and injury evidence of PW-9; co-villagers' statements
witness_credibility: PW-1 found reliable and independent; trial court found him trustworthy with nothing to falsely implicate his master; his silence explained by fear. PW-2 corroborative; PW-9 injuries support prosecution story
post_offence_conduct: Accused came to the scene of the body and enquired; no other post-offence conduct noted
trial_duration: offence: 29.03.2000; trial judgment: 18.03.2006; High Court: 26.09.2006; Supreme Court: 3 May 2013
legal_representation: Appellant: Pandit Parmanand Katara (senior counsel) with Abhishek Sharma, C.K. Sucharita, Kusum Lata Sharma. State: Navnit Kumar, Avijit Roy (Corporate Law Group)
investigation_status: FIR registered; charge-sheet filed under ss.376 and 302 IPC; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted; death for s.302 and life RI for s.376. High Court: conviction confirmed, death altered to life, s.376 altered to 7 years. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: PW-1's evidence is reliable and corroborated by PW-2 and PW-9; sentence commuted to life imprisonment cannot lead to automatic release after 14 years
defence_argument: PW-1's evidence unreliable; no mark of sexual violence so s.376 conviction unsustainable; after commutation to life the accused should have been released after 14 years
legal_principle_applied: Life imprisonment means imprisonment for the whole of life subject to executive remission under Arts 72 and 161; where death is commuted, remission must be exercised cautiously considering gravity of offence; medical and eyewitness evidence assessed for reliability
precedent_relied_upon: Life Convict @ Khoka Prasanta Sen v. B.K. Srivastava (2013) 3 SCC 425; Mohinder Singh v. State of Punjab (2013) 3 SCC 294; Sangeet v. State of Haryana (2013) 2 SCC 452; Rameshbhai Chandubhai Rathod (2) v. State of Gujarat (2011) 2 SCC 764; Chhote Lal v. State of MP (2011) 8 SCR 239; Mulla v. State of UP (2010) 3 SCC 508; Maru Ram v. Union of India (1981) 1 SCC 107; State of MP v. Ratan Singh (1976) 3 SCC 470; Gopal Vinayak Godse v. State of Maharashtra AIR 1961 SC 600; Swami Shraddananda (2) v. State of Karnataka (2008) 13 SCC 767; Sahib Hussain v. State of Rajasthan 2013 (6) Scale 219
sentencing_rationale: Death sentence commuted to life imprisonment by the High Court because of the accused's young age and the case not being rarest of rare; Supreme Court upheld this and rejected claim of release after 14 years
judicial_mitigating_factors: Young age of accused (33), as noted by the High Court and not contested by the Supreme Court
judicial_aggravating_factors: Heinous nature of rape and murder and disposal of body in bushes, noted by the Supreme Court while describing the sentence
